newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania vote firm despite security, redtape - OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Albania vote firm despite security, redtape - OSCE.

text.p: A top OSCE official said on Friday there was no plan to delay June 29 elections intended to restore stability in Albania, despite security concerns and foot-dragging by Albanian parties on technical details.

Asked if the elections should be postponed, Herbert Grubmayr, the OSCE administrator in Albania, said, "We have analysed this situation and most of our people agreed it would not really help the situation.
"It would just heighten tensions. It might worsen the situation if there is a postponement and it would not make sense -- not for the Albanians and not for us," he told Reuters in an interview.
Earlier this week a senior Western diplomat told Reuters the elections might have to be delayed by a week or two but such a proposal was not under active consideration.

"I think the international community would not be averse to slippage of a week or two...which might be required for technical reasons," the diplomat said, adding that there was no support for a longer delay as sought by some Albanian parties.
"This country has some major economic problems and the temporary government is not able to take decisions to get it back on its feet," the diplomat said.

Grubmayr spoke towards the end of the first week of the poll-monitoring mission in which experts from the OSCE (Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe), have fanned out around a country still tense after an outbreak of rioting and looting in March.

The riots were sparked by people who lost life savings in shady pyramid investment schemes and undermined government confidence, forcing early elections and installation of an interim government of national reconciliation.
Grubmayr, resident deputy to OSCE Albania envoy Franz Vranitzky, said teams of more than two dozen vote experts had found local authorities to be cooperative.
"We have not found any examples of resistance or lack of cooperation," he said.

But he said security remained a major concern in parts of Albania and added that Albanian political parties had hindered preparations by failing to provide essential information, such as the order in which party names should appear on ballots.
"We have problems to get basic information for materials we want to purchase or get printed abroad," Grubmayr said.
"We cannot make the...sequence of the parties on the ballot paper, they have to do it. We're pushing them now...saying that by Monday we want to have that -- that it's essential."

Grubmayr said it should be possible to deal with other logistical matters, such as obtaining 200 vehicles to ferry 400 short-term observers to polling places on election day. He said the OSCE had a budget of 28 million Austrian schillings (about $2.5 million) for the elections and that the OSCE's 54 member states and other organisations should cover other costs.
He said security in many areas had been improved by the presence of the 6,000-strong Italian-led multinational force, but was still a major concern.

"We cannot say so far which parts of the territory of Albania we can really reach," he said. "The security situation is very volatile, one day it might be safe and another day not, so we will have to go by trial and error procedures."
He added that the OSCE was adamant that it would not take over the running of the elections, which he said was Albania's concern.
"We are told they need two soldiers and two observers for each polling station and that would be nearly 9,000 (observers)," Grubmayr said.
"That would be clearly illusory. This is an independent country, it is not a colony. We do not organise the elections, the Albanians organise the elections."
